:::{.def}

While last section used synthetic data, projects usually require real data.

In this section, we look at three ways to obtain data: [Torchvision built-in datasets](https://pytorch.org/vision/stable/datasets.html), [Hugging Face Hub](https://huggingface.co/datasets), and your own data, read with a custom class.

:::

## Our working dataset: EuroSAT

[EuroSAT](https://github.com/phelber/eurosat) [@8736785] is a set of 27,000 small (64 × 64 pixels) RGB patches from [Sentinel-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentinel-2) images, each labelled with one of 10 land-use classes. It is distributed under an MIT licence.

It is a good fit for us: real research data (remote sensing), yet small enough to download and train on quickly, even on modest GPUs.

## Setup

By default, Hugging Face downloads datasets into [~/.cache/huggingface/hub]{.codelike} and, once processed, saves them in [~/.cache/huggingface/datasets]{.codelike}. To avoid each downloading and writing the same data, we can set the `HF_HUB_CACHE` and `HF_DATASETS_CACHE` environment variables to a shared location in [/project]{.codelike}:

```{.python}
import os
os.environ["HF_HUB_CACHE"] = "/project/def-sponsor00/hub"
os.environ["HF_DATASETS_CACHE"] = "/project/def-sponsor00/datasets"
```

:::{.notenoit}

Note that you need to do this **before** importing any Hugging Face package.

If you use this method to share data among collaborators, a better option is to have everyone set the environment variables directly, for instance by adding to their [.bashrc]{.codelike} file:

```{.bash}
export HF_HUB_CACHE="/project/def-sponsor00/hub"
export HF_DATASETS_CACHE="/project/def-sponsor00/datasets"
```

Avoid sharing `HF_HOME` across users as it might contain tokens and other sensitive information.

:::

```{python}
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path

import datasets as hf
import torch
from torch.utils.data import Dataset, random_split
from matplotlib import pyplot as plt
from PIL import Image
from torchvision.datasets import EuroSAT
```

- `torch.utils.data` holds the dataset machinery: the [`Dataset`](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/data.html) base class and `random_split`.
- `torchvision.datasets` provides ready-made vision datasets, `EuroSAT` among them.
- `datasets` is the Hugging Face data library.
- `PIL.Image` opens image files and `Counter` will tally labels.

## Torchvision datasets

`torchvision.datasets` provides built-in computer vision datasets and base classes. Because they subclass `torch.utils.data.Dataset`, they implement the functions `__init__` (instantiating the class), `__len__` (returning the number of samples in the dataset) and `__getitem__` (returning one sample at a time). This means that you can pass them directly to the PyTorch DataLoader machinery for batching, shuffling, and parallel loading.

```{python}
#| echo: false
root = Path("data")
```

```{.python}
root = Path("/project/def-sponsor00/data")
```

```{python}
eurosat = EuroSAT(root=root, download=True)
```

`download=True` fetches and extracts the archive into the chosen root directory (here [/project/def-sponsor00/data]{.codelike}) on the first run, then detects the files and skips the download. On disk, this is the classic layout, one folder per class:

```

/project/def-sponsor00/data/eurosat/2750/AnnualCrop/AnnualCrop_1.jpg
/project/def-sponsor00/data/eurosat/2750/AnnualCrop/AnnualCrop_2.jpg
/project/def-sponsor00/data/eurosat/2750/AnnualCrop/AnnualCrop_3.jpg
...
/project/def-sponsor00/data/eurosat/2750/Forest/Forest_1.jpg
/project/def-sponsor00/data/eurosat/2750/Forest/Forest_2.jpg
/project/def-sponsor00/data/eurosat/2750/Forest/Forest_3.jpg
...

```

Let's explore the dataset:

```{python}
print(eurosat)
```

```{python}
print(len(eurosat), "images")
```

```{python}
print(eurosat.classes)
```

```{python}
print(len(eurosat.classes))
```

When the dataset is created, initialization scans the file names. To read in images, you index the dataset object:

```{python}
img, label = eurosat[0]
```

Images are stored as PIL images, not tensors. They will be converted to tensors in preprocessing:

```{python}
print(type(img).__name__, img.size, img.mode)
```

`eurosat.classes` is a list of the 10 classes of land-use sorted alphabetically. The label associated with each image is the index of the class it belongs to:

```{python}
print(label, eurosat.classes[label])
print(eurosat[4000][1], eurosat.classes[eurosat[4000][1]])
print(eurosat[9000][1], eurosat.classes[eurosat[9000][1]])
print(eurosat[12000][1], eurosat.classes[eurosat[12000][1]])
```

Let's display one image for each class:

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 5, figsize=(12, 5))
for ax, cls in zip(axes.flat, range(len(eurosat.classes))):
	img, _ = eurosat[eurosat.targets.index(cls)]
	ax.imshow(img)
	ax.set_title(eurosat.classes[cls], fontsize=9)
	ax.axis("off")
```

### Class balance

You should never trust a dataset to be balanced. Let's check how balanced our dataset is.

`eurosat.targets` holds the labels. Let's print the total per class:

```{python}
counts = Counter(eurosat.targets)
for i, name in enumerate(eurosat.classes):
	print(f"{name:>22} {counts[i]}")  # >22 right-aligns for a nicer display
```

We can visualize it with a quick histogram:

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.barh(eurosat.classes, [counts[c] for c in range(10)])
ax.set_xlabel("Number of images")
```

EuroSAT has 2,000 to 3,000 images per class: a mild imbalance. When classes are heavily skewed, a high accuracy can hide a model that ignores the rare classes entirely; we will come back to this when evaluating models.

### Train and validation sets

[Never evaluate a model on data it learned from.]{.emph}

We randomly split EuroSAT, 80% for training and 20% for validation:

```{python}
train, val = random_split(
	eurosat, [0.8, 0.2], generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(42)
)
print(f"Training set size: {len(train)} items\nValidation set size: {len(val)} items\nType: {type(train).__name__}")
```

- `random_split` returns two `Subset` objects: thin views holding lists of indices from `eurosat`. No image is copied and the dataset characteristics (`__init__`, `__len__`, and `__getitem__` are maintained).
- The seeded generator makes the shuffle reproducible.

:::{.note}

`random_split` does not respect class balance. With EuroSAT's mild imbalance this hardly matters, but on small or heavily skewed data, draw a stratified split yourself (same class proportions in both parts).

The rest of the course must evaluate on this exact validation set, or the results from different sections would not be comparable. Let's save the index lists as a [split.pt]{.codelike} file in our data directory:


## Hugging Face Hub

[Hugging Face datasets Hub](https://huggingface.co/datasets) mirrors thousands of datasets and researchers increasingly share their data there. The [datasets library](https://github.com/huggingface/datasets) downloads and caches them, carries metadata along, preprocesses them in parallel, and streams datasets too big to fit on disk.

There are [118 EuroSAT datasets](https://huggingface.co/datasets?search=eurosat) on HF. [blanchon/EuroSAT_RGB](https://huggingface.co/datasets/blanchon/EuroSAT_RGB) is by far the most popular and the most downloaded of them. If you look at the associated paper, you will see that it is [the EuroSAT description paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.00029) [@8736785]. This thus seems like the perfect dataset to use:

```{python}
eurosat_hf = hf.load_dataset("blanchon/EuroSAT_RGB")
print(type(eurosat_hf))
print(eurosat_hf)
```

The first call downloads the data into [/project/def-sponsor00/datasets]{.codelike} and converts it into Apache Arrow files; later calls hit the cache and return instantly. We get a `DatasetDict` of named splits: this copy of EuroSAT comes pre-split into train/validation/test.

Unlike in the Torchvision dataset, the labels come with the data (so they aren't based on file indexing):

```{python}
train_hf = eurosat_hf["train"]
print(train_hf.features)
```

```{python}
label_meta = train_hf.features["label"]
print(label_meta.names)
```

```{python}
print(train_hf[0])
```

```{python}
print(train_hf[0]["image"])
```

```{python}
print(train_hf[0]["label"])
```

```{python}
print(train_hf[0]["filename"])
```

The [`map()`](https://huggingface.co/docs/datasets/v5.2.0/package_reference/main_classes#datasets.Dataset.map) method applies a function to every item in the dataset and caches the result on disk, keyed by a fingerprint of the function.

For instance, to add a new feature called "label_name" to `train_hf` which contains the class names as string of the labels (using [Hugging Face datasets `int2str()`](https://huggingface.co/docs/datasets/v5.2.0/package_reference/main_classes#datasets.ClassLabel.int2str)), we can run:

```{python}
def add_label_name(example):
	return {"label_name": label_meta.int2str(example["label"])}

train_hf = train_hf.map(add_label_name)
print(train_hf[0]["label_name"])
```

You can use `map()` in parallel by setting a value to the `num_proc` argument.

:::{.note}

HF datasets satisfy the same `__init__`/`__len__`/`__getitem__` class structure, so they plug into the same DataLoaders as everything else.

Using `with_format("torch")` returns the labels directly as tensors.

:::

If you don't want to download the data files, you can pass `streaming=True` to `hf.load_dataset()`:

```{python}
stream = hf.load_dataset("blanchon/EuroSAT_RGB", split="train", streaming=True)
first = next(iter(stream))
print(first["filename"])
```

This is useful to inspect datasets without downloading them, to save storage space for very large datasets, or when the processing pipeline is slow enough that the added network speed doesn't become a bottleneck.

## Torchvision vs HF datasets

While both are equally convenient, there are key differences in design philosophies, file formats, and caching architectures between Torchvision and Hugging Face datasets that can lead to massive differences in disk usage and speed.

For our dataset, the Torchvision files take up ~90 MiB of storage while the Hugging Face files take up ~770 MiB.

But this difference in storage comes with an efficiency trade-off: Torchvision datasets are designed to save bandwidth and storage for standard vision benchmarks, whereas Hugging Face datasets are engineered for high-performance data processing, random access, and zero-copy memory mapping.

**Torchvision** downloads datasets in their native, highly-compressed distribution formats such as `.tar`, `.zip`, `.gz`, or raw PNG/JPEG images. PyTorch reads these archives directly or extracts them minimally.

**Hugging Face** converts and caches datasets into **Apache Arrow** files. Arrow is an in-memory columnar format optimized for blazing-fast data retrieval, filtering, and machine learning pipelines. This layout sacrifices storage space to maximize read speed and minimize CPU overhead during training. Additionally, the memory-mapping done by Apache Arrow allows your operating system to map the dataset on disk directly into virtual memory: instead of loading a 50GB dataset into your physical RAM (which would crash your computer), your script reads it straight from the disk as if it were in memory. For this to work efficiently without massive CPU stuttering, the data on disk must be structured in a predictable, aligned layout rather than being tightly squeezed inside a compressed archive that requires sequential decompression.

## Custom Dataset

The most common situation of all: a folder of images on your machine, arranged somehow, that you need to train on. First, organize the images to have one folder per class. Then create a subclass to `Dataset` that processes your images adequately. With nice, clean data, it could look like this:

```{python}
class ImageFiles(Dataset):
	"""Images in one subfolder per class under root; labels from folder names."""

	def __init__(self, root, transform=None, extensions=(".jpg", ".jpeg", ".png")):
		root = root
		# sorted: alphabetical class names give deterministic, portable label indices
		self.classes = sorted(p.name for p in root.iterdir() if p.is_dir())
		self.class_to_idx = {name: i for i, name in enumerate(self.classes)}
		self.transform = transform
		# scan the file list once walking class by class
		self.samples = [
			(path, label)
			for label, name in enumerate(self.classes)
			for path in sorted((root / name).iterdir())
			if path.suffix.lower() in extensions
		]

	def __len__(self):
		return len(self.samples)

	def __getitem__(self, index):
		path, label = self.samples[index]
		# convert("RGB"): stray grayscale or RGBA files should not crash a training run
		img = Image.open(path).convert("RGB")
		if self.transform is not None:  # used on the preprocessing page
			img = self.transform(img)
		return img, label
```

- `__init__` scans the tree once and stores `(path, label)` pairs: paths only, no image is opened.
- `__getitem__` opens one image per call: decoding on demand is what will let worker processes parallelize the reading.
- `transform` is the hook where preprocessing will plug in.

Let's point it at the EuroSAT tree:

```{python}
eurosat_custom = ImageFiles(root / "eurosat" / "2750")
img, label = eurosat_custom[0]
print(len(eurosat_custom), "images,", len(eurosat_custom.classes), "classes")
print(type(img).__name__, img.size, "->", label, eurosat_custom.classes[label])
```

### Comparison with Torchvision

```{python}
print(eurosat_custom.classes == eurosat.classes)
```

```{python}
print([lbl for _, lbl in eurosat_custom.samples] == eurosat.targets)
```

Our dataset agrees with Torchvision's reader, class for class and label for label. If your data is more messy, you can adapt this class to transform and tidy it. Our section on [data preprocessing](../jxai/jxai_preprocess.qmd) in our [deep learning course with the JAX AI stack](../top_jxai.qmd) goes into this in a lot more details.
